It is entirely possible that someone who failed to convince his contemporaries or win them over will succeed in convincing later generations, and that a person universally regarded as a criminal in one age will be transformed into a hero many centuries after his death.

Generalizing further, we can say that there is no final knowledge of humanity and its historical, social, and political world—and that there can be none—so long as neither humanity nor its world has itself become final.
Nature has been complete and unchanging “for ever and ever.” It will eternally remain what it is now.
Only our knowledge of nature is partial and incomplete, and so only that knowledge changes and develops. This is why knowledge of nature can be genuine knowledge even while remaining incomplete.
With humanity, however, it is not merely our knowledge that is incomplete. Humanity itself is “incomplete,” and humanity itself changes.
Everything we currently know about the human being is therefore little more than a question mark or a subject for investigation—in the final analysis, an opinion rather than genuine knowledge.
An example will make this clearer.
Suppose we want to study cows and chickens but have available only a calf and a chick.
We might then establish that cows have no horns and chickens are covered in yellow down.
Those observations would be correct with respect to the creatures we are actually studying.
But they would be false of cows and chickens in general.
We can establish their falsity only because we are able to observe the complete developmental cycle of these animals—a cycle that repeats itself “eternally” and without variation.
The developmental cycle of humanity, by contrast, is plainly not complete, and in any case there can be no question of its repeating itself.

We therefore cannot know whether what we have learned about humanity so far is genuine knowledge or merely an opinion that happens to be valid during a certain period and from a particular point of view but is not valid in general.
In other words, our present knowledge of humanity is about as final as our knowledge of cows would be if we had studied only calves.
We can say that Hegel was the first to become conscious of the existence of real and historical struggle and work—that is, of technical and political processes that are genuinely dialectical.
Hegel understood the importance of this fact for philosophy and for knowledge in general.

But he himself had no reason to fear the troubling consequences that might follow from it. He believed that the process of human development had already been completed in his own time, and therefore that historical dialectic gave him both the right and the ability to distinguish mere opinions from true or false knowledge.
Since Marx, however, we have finally understood that Hegel was mistaken on this point: the historical process had not ended, and it still has not ended.
All post-Hegelian thinkers agree on this.

Yet those among them who remain Hegel’s followers—whether consciously or without realizing it—and who come from the ranks of the bourgeoisie generally reject the idea of an end of history. They assume instead that the historical process will continue “forever.”

Once they admit this, however, they are forced to accept all the troubling consequences of historical dialectic and ultimately to abandon the very idea of truth and knowledge, reducing everything to social opinion.
One can then speak of true and false, normal and pathological, criminal and heroic only by placing them within specific conditions of space and time.
What is valid here and now may be false elsewhere and later, and vice versa.
There would therefore be no possible way of reaching final knowledge.

This bourgeois—or, if one prefers, “vulgar”—sociologism thus ends in complete scepticism and complements the sceptical “positivism” we encountered when discussing our cognitive grasp of the natural world.
In the earlier case, scepticism resulted from ignoring the real dialectic of work. Here, on the contrary, it results from discovering the real dialectic of struggle.
But in both cases the result is exactly the same: the rejection of knowledge and the “liberal” demand that all opinions be granted equal rights.
Genuine philosophy clearly cannot rest content with this sceptical “sociologism.”

As the true heir of Hegelianism, Marxism-Leninism-Stalinism did not rest content with it either. On the contrary, while continuing to begin from Hegel, it tried to preserve the idea of true knowledge.

Once Marx understood that the historical process had not yet come to an end in Hegel’s time—or even in his own—he nevertheless kept Hegel’s idea of an end of history. He therefore held that final and complete human knowledge of humanity could be achieved only by the human being of communist society, who brings historical development to its completion.

According to Marx, as according to Hegel, final and perfect knowledge—absolute truth—can be attained only at “the end of time.” This would be total knowledge, the knowledge of everything, or wisdom. But Marx now faced a question Hegel had never asked: how can we distinguish partial—that is, philosophical—knowledge from mere opinion? This is precisely the problem we are dealing with here. And Marx found the only possible solution in Hegel’s own discovery: the discovery of historical dialectic.

To begin with, knowledge of historical dialectic allows the philosopher to question everything that people unfamiliar with dialectic normally regard as definitively true or false—that is, as genuine knowledge. The philosopher knows that, until it has been subjected to dialectical testing, such “knowledge” is really nothing more than an opinion, whether private or generally accepted—or, as Marx likes to call it, an ideology. Only through the real, historical dialectic can the philosopher transform an “ideology” into genuine, though partial, knowledge of humanity and nature.

We must first regard as ideological any claim that, at a particular historical moment, is accepted as true by the state and society in which it arose. The study of historical dialectic shows that such views are socially recognized as true not simply—and not primarily—because they correspond, either genuinely or apparently, to the facts. They are accepted above all because, at that moment, they serve the “interests” of a particular state by helping to preserve and stabilize it.

But pre-communist states do not represent the whole society they organize. They represent one particular class within it. So we can say that an “ideology” is treated as genuine knowledge rather than as a questionable opinion because it expresses the interests of the ruling social class at a particular time.

The first task of dialectical philosophy is therefore to show that the “knowledge” presented to it is, in the end, only a class opinion—in other words, an ideology. Its second task is to separate what is false in that ideology from what is true: to isolate the element within it that really is knowledge.

When ideologies concern our knowledge of nature, they can be settled through experimental and technical testing—that is, through real, dialectical work. Ideologies about nature contain, on the one hand, “hypotheses”: claims about what already exists. On the other hand, they contain “projects”: claims about what ought to be created.

In the first case, the question of truth, and therefore of knowledge, is settled through real, active experiment. In the second, the truth of the claim is itself made real through technology. In both cases, all the philosopher has to do is record the result of the real, physical interaction between human knowledge and natural reality. Taken in the broadest sense, this interaction is what we call work.

Things become more difficult and more controversial when an ideology concerns our knowledge of the human world—the social, political, or historical world. Here we are dealing with “ideology” in the narrower and proper sense of the word.

If the state and its ruling class remained eternally unchanged, the political testing of ideologies about humanity would be no different from the technical testing of ideologies about nature. But historical dialectic shows that this is not what actually happens.

The whole difficulty comes from the fact that the human world can undergo radical and fundamental change. Genuine revolutions are possible within it, not merely changes that leave its basic identity intact.

The study of historical dialectic shows that revolutionary changes in society are always preceded by the appearance of an ideology opposed to the one accepted by the pre-revolutionary society. A pre-revolutionary society is therefore marked by the presence of two contradictory and mutually exclusive ideologies, corresponding to the class contradictions developing within it.

When the philosopher looks at a pre-revolutionary society, he consequently finds himself in much the same situation as Plato when he was faced with incompatible “myths.” He knows that he is dealing with opinions—ideologies—and looks to dialectic for a way of moving from them toward knowledge.
But his method will be radically different from Plato’s.
A choice has to be made between the two opposing ideologies. Let us begin with the newly emerging revolutionary ideology.

If we find that it disappears without changing the existing forms of society and the state, we will regard it as a false opinion. The older ideology, by contrast, can still be regarded as possibly true—at least for as long as it continues to survive the test.
But if the revolutionary ideology triumphs through a process of revolutionary struggle, the situation must be judged differently.

We must first compare the new revolutionary ideology with the old pre-revolutionary one and identify what they have in common. We must then ask whether this common element is preserved in the ideology that the post-revolutionary society accepts as true.
If it is not preserved, we can regard it as “ideology” in the narrow sense: a false opinion that had been treated as true only because it served the temporary interests of a particular social class.

If, however, the common element survives into the post-revolutionary ideology as well, then it has not yet been refuted. It can therefore be treated as a possibly true opinion—or, more precisely, as a claim that still remains open to question.

But the revolutionary ideology contains something more than what it shares with the old ideology. It also contains something fundamentally new, something that distinguishes it from the old ideology and directly contradicts it.
We can call this new element the revolutionary idea contained within the ideology.

It is over this idea that the revolutionary struggle takes place. The result of that struggle is the transformation of the entire social and political order and the creation of a new, post-revolutionary state and society.
To determine what is true and false in this “idea,” we must therefore compare it with the ideology adopted by the new state.

Historical dialectic shows that the revolutionary idea is never incorporated into the post-revolutionary ideology in its entirety. The people who “made” the revolution are often almost as hostile to its final outcome as the defenders of the old social and political order.
Because the new state does not fully accept everything they had regarded as definitively true.

The outcome of a revolution never comes down entirely on the side of the revolutionary “antithesis” and entirely against the pre-revolutionary “thesis.” What emerges instead is a kind of synthesis, in which thesis and antithesis neutralize one another, so to speak, enter into a “chemical compound,” and form a new social and political body.

The “pure” revolutionaries may see this synthesis as a “betrayal” of the revolutionary idea. But the philosopher will regard as true knowledge only those parts of the revolutionary idea that survive within the synthesis.

Whatever disappears during the revolutionary process must therefore be treated as “revolutionary ideology”: an opinion which, although revolutionary, was just as false as the opposing pre-revolutionary opinion that also perished in the struggle.

Of course, the post-revolutionary “synthesis” is not final. If the revolution has not abolished all social contradictions, the post-revolutionary ideology will simply become a new “thesis.” Sooner or later it will generate a new revolutionary “antithesis,” and their real struggle will produce another post-revolutionary synthesis.
And so the process continues, until communist society is reached.

For this reason, the post-revolutionary “truth,” taken as a whole, is still only an ideology from the philosopher’s point of view. It is not yet final knowledge. But whatever survives from the revolutionary idea within the new synthesis can be regarded as genuine knowledge: partial, certainly, but definitive.
In other words, revolutionary testing does for our knowledge of humanity what technical testing does for our knowledge of nature.
The merely political test mentioned earlier is comparable to a passive “experiment”—that is, to experience based simply on observing what exists. It cannot give us definitive knowledge either.
Only a test through revolution can do that.
We can regard as true only what has, first, been put up for “decision” in a revolutionary struggle and, second, survived that struggle.
The analogy with technical testing is easy to see. In both cases we are dealing not with passive observation but with active interaction. In both cases reality itself settles the question.

The revolutionary idea “makes” the new state. To the extent that the historical world accepts that state—allows it to become and remain real—we can regard the idea as definitively true. And we must accept, without objection, the “corrections” that the revolutionary realization of the idea makes to the idea itself, just as we must accept the corrections that technical realization makes to an initial design.
We can now summarize the argument.
The philosopher must first distinguish between statements about the natural world and statements about the human world.

Knowledge of the real dialectic of work forces the philosopher to question every statement of the first kind until it has undergone experimental testing. But knowledge of the character of this dialectic also allows him to extract from the mass of questionable “opinions” a body of genuine knowledge, partial though it may be.
To do this, he divides these opinions into “hypotheses” and “projects,” depending on whether they concern something that already exists or something that is to be made.
The “hypotheses” are tested through experiment—through real, physical interaction between theory and reality. The “project” is tested by actually realizing it through technology.

When it comes to statements about the human world, knowledge of the real dialectic of struggle likewise forces the philosopher to treat them initially not as scientific knowledge but as questionable opinions or “ideologies” reflecting the vital interests of some social class.
Yet here too, knowledge of the character of the real historical dialectic makes it possible to separate genuine, though partial, and nevertheless definitive knowledge from the mass of ideologies.
We reach this knowledge by studying the revolutionary testing of ideologies.
On the basis of such a study, the philosopher can distinguish three elements within an ideology, understood in the broad sense:
First, what we can call “ideology” in the narrow sense: a questionable opinion—or, by analogy with knowledge of nature, a “hypothesis.”
Second, what corresponds to a “project”: the idea contained within the revolutionary ideology.
Third, the genuine, though partial, knowledge expressed in some way by that idea.
By comparing the pre-revolutionary ideology—the thesis—with the revolutionary ideology—the antithesis—we can identify what they have in common.
This common element clearly concerns something both sides regard as already existing within the historical world in question. For the philosopher, it is therefore a hypothesis about that world.
But precisely because no revolutionary struggle is taking place over this shared claim, it has not yet undergone dialectical testing. It therefore remains open to question.
If we later discover that this common claim is absent from the post-revolutionary ideology, or is explicitly rejected by it, we must regard the claim as false.

If, on the other hand, it survives the revolution, we must still regard it as unproven—at least until some future revolutionary situation puts it to the test through a struggle between an ideology that retains the claim and a new ideology that denies it.
But let us return to the thesis and antithesis.
Once we have removed what they share, what remains is the pure contradiction between a claim made by the pre-revolutionary ideology and the opposing claim made by the revolutionary ideology.
This new claim within the revolutionary ideology is its “idea.”
A real struggle rages around this idea. Society is revolutionized through the idea and through the struggle fought over it.
We can therefore say that the new society stands in the same relation to this idea as a newly built machine stands to its design.
